div.head: Ine 23.1
div.ab: Gif he ðonne mægleas sie, healf kyninge, healf se gesið.
Gif he ðonne mægles sy, healf cyninge, healf se gesið.
Gyf he ðonne mægleas sy, half cyning, half se gesið.
Si parentes non habeat, dimidiam habeat rex, dimidiam congildones (consocii).
Gif he ðonne mægleas sie, healf kyninge, healf se gesið.
Gif he ðonne mægleas sie, healf kyninge, healf se gesið.
Wenn jener [Erschlagene] jedoch sippenlos ist, [gehört das Wergeld] halb dem Könige, halb [empfängt es] der Genoss[enverband?].
But if that [slain man] is without kin, [the wergeld belongs] half to the king; half [is received by] the companion[ship?].
If he has no relatives, the king shall have one-half and the magnate shall have the other.
If, however, he is without kinsmen, half [goes to] the king, half to the gesith.
If he is without kinsmen, half to the king and half to the nobleman [under whose protection he has been residing].

‘der König’ B Q; Thorpe will kyningc lesen (was aber für c. 925 wohl nicht nachgewiesen ist) gemäss folgendem Nominativ. Allein in diesem ellipsenreichen Stile ist das Hinzudenken von ‘gehört’ zum ersten und von ‘empfängt’ zur zweiten Satzhälfte möglich

‘The king’ B Q; Thorpe wants to read kyningc (which, however, is probably not attested for c. 925) in accordance with the following nominative. But in this style, rich in ellipses, it is possible to supply ‘belongs’ in the first half of the sentence and ‘receives’ in the second

nicht ‘Königs Gefolge’, wie Q spät. Rez., wohl die Bed. comes annehmend, versteht; danach Earle Landchar. lxix. Auch Phillpotts Kindred 208 versteht ‘Adligen’. Vgl. Gl Genossenschaft 4a; Gefolgsadel 31; Sippe 26b. ‘Teilnehmer der Handelsfahrt’ versteht Doren Kaufmannsgilden 6, den verantwortlichen Gastfreund des fremden Kaufmanns am Englischen Markte Price. Allein der entsprechende Satz Af 28 spricht gegen die Beschränkung der Genossen auf Fremde

not ‘king’s retinue’, as Q, later recension, understands it, probably assuming the meaning comes; followed by Earle Landchar. lxix. Phillpotts Kindred 208 also understands ‘nobleman’. Cf. Gl Genossenschaft 4a; Gefolgsadel 31; Sippe 26b. Doren Kaufmannsgilden 6 understands ‘participants in the trading voyage’, Price the foreign merchant’s responsible host at the English market. But the corresponding sentence Af 28 tells against restricting the associates to foreigners

i.e. the man under whose protection he has been. Liebermann connects this law with Alf. cap. 31, and understands se gesið to be equivalent to þam gegildan (Alf. cap. 31), but the two cases are not really parallel. There is no previous reference here to gegildan as there is in Alf. cap. 30, while in the latter case it is not stated that the person under discussion is a foreigner. Further, Gif hit ðonne abbod sie of the following clause (23 § 2) clearly carries on the sense of healf se gesið, and must refer to the person in authority over the dead man. For the use of gesið cf. cap. 50. ‘Squire’ might be a better trans. but the authority implied is over persons rather than land.

note.label: gesith
note.seg: Liebermann takes gesith here in the general sense of “companion”, comparing the gegildan of Alfred 31, but it is more probable that Attenborough is right in taking it as “the man under whose protection he has been”, which makes better sense of the next clause. On gesith, see also p. 396, n. 4.
